Hypergeometric stopping test for prioritised screening

Source: R/doc-screen-stop.R
gr_stop_test.Rd

After each screened record, tests the null hypothesis that recall is still below target, given what has been screened and how many records are left. Screening may stop at the first record where the p-value falls below alpha. This is the test of Callaghan and Muller-Hansen (2020), computed with stats::phyper(). It is for prioritised screening only (records read in ranked order, as hr_baseline_ranker() simulates); a one-pass screen that reads every record has no stopping point to choose.

Usage

gr_stop_test(screened_order, target = 0.95, alpha = 0.05, n_total = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'gr_stop_test'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

screened_order

The relevance of the records in the order they were screened: logical, or numeric 0 and 1 (1 = relevant). Records not yet screened may follow as NA at the end, and count toward n_total. An hr_baseline_ranker() result is also accepted, and its whole simulated order is tested.

target

Recall level, strictly between 0 and 1.

alpha

Significance level, strictly between 0 and 1.

n_total

Total number of records, screened or not. Defaults to the length of screened_order.

x

A gr_stop_test.

...

Not used.

Value

A gr_stop_test, a list with:

  • steps: one row per screened record, with n_screened, relevant_found, p_value and reject (p below alpha).

  • stop_at: the first n_screened with reject, or NA when the test never rejects.

  • relevant_at_stop and recall_at_stop: the relevant records found by then and, when every record's relevance is known, the recall reached there.

  • work_saved: 1 - stop_at / n_total.

  • target, alpha, n_total and n_screened.

Details

The test. Let N be the number of records, t the number screened so far and r the relevant records among them. Recall r / R is below target only if the total number of relevant records R is at least K = floor(r / target) + 1. Take the last m screened records as if they were a random draw from the N - t + m records that were unscreened before them, with k relevant among them. Under the null, at least K - (r - k) of those N - t + m records are relevant, and the chance of seeing k or fewer in the draw is at most the hypergeometric probability

p(m) = P(X <= k), X ~ Hypergeometric(N - t + m records, K - (r - k) relevant, m drawn),

which is phyper(k, K - r + k, N - t + m - (K - r + k), m). The p-value after t records is the smallest p(m) over m = 1, ..., t, as in the authors' treatment of already screened records as a sample. When fewer than K - r records are left unscreened, the null cannot hold and p is 0.

Caveats. The ranked records are not a random draw. A working ranker reads the most likely relevant of the remaining records first, so the window is richer in relevant records than a random draw from them would be. That makes the test cautious when the ranker works and unreliable when it ranks worse than chance. The minimum over m and the look after every record are not corrected for repeated testing, as in the original method. No stopping rule is standard; report the rule and its settings with the result.

References

Callaghan, M. W. and Muller-Hansen, F. (2020). Statistical stopping criteria for automated screening in systematic reviews. Systematic Reviews 9, 273.

See also

hr_baseline_ranker() for a simulated screening order.

Examples

# 1,000 records: 100 relevant found first, then 400 irrelevant in a row.
seen <- c(rep(1, 100), rep(0, 400), rep(NA, 500))
st <- gr_stop_test(seen)
st
#> <gr_stop_test> recall target 0.95, alpha 0.05, 500 of 1000 records screened
#>   safe to stop after 453 records (100 relevant found), work saved 0.547
# At 500 screened, the last 400 records hold no relevant ones; under the
# null at least 6 relevant records were among the 900 left before them.
prod((500 - 0:5) / (900 - 0:5))
#> [1] 0.02900956
st$steps$p_value[500]
#> [1] 0.02900956
